content.text: Ford Transit V348 2.2 Duratorq Puma Engine Failure Representative Case Study Ford Transit 2.2 Engine Failure - Why Downtime Cost More Than the Engine A premium visual breakdown of black smoke, wasted DPF repairs, bore wash from failed injectors, and the decision to fit a reconditioned engine with turbo - prioritising uptime over repair cost. "Black smoke pouring out the back. Failed the MOT on emissions. The driver said it was using a litre of oil every 500 miles. We'd already spent £1,200 on a new DPF and EGR valve. Three months later, the same problems came back. That's when the mechanic said, 'The injectors are wrecked. They've washed the bores. The rings are gone. You need an engine.'" Compare Transit Engine Quotes See the Failure Timeline 105k First symptom £1,200 Wasted repairs £3,800 Engine fitted £4,600 Final total 18 mo Warranty Case summary A 2013 Transit with 110,000 miles - fleet vehicle for courier work. The fleet manager first noticed black smoke from one of the Transits under acceleration. The driver reported a gradual loss of power, particularly up hills. The van failed its MOT on emissions. An independent garage diagnosed a clogged DPF and failing EGR valve - £1,200 later, the problems returned within three months. Model Ford Transit V348 Year 2013 Engine 2.2 Duratorq (Puma) - 4-cylinder turbo diesel Mileage at first symptom 105,000 miles Mileage at failure 110,000 miles Usage Fleet vehicle - courier work, daily use Disclaimer: This is a representative scenario based on common failure patterns observed across Ford Duratorq diesel family quote requests on Engines Market in 2025 [ESTIMATED - using Ford DV6 1.6 TDCi enquiry data (n=780) and Ford Duratorq 2.2 TDCi (n=300) as proxy], combined with workshop consensus and KNOWN FAILURE PATTERNS data. Individual outcomes vary. The first clue Black smoke under acceleration - treated as a DPF issue, not injectors. The fleet manager first noticed black smoke from the Transit under acceleration. The driver reported a gradual loss of power, particularly up hills. The van failed its MOT on emissions. An independent garage diagnosed a clogged DPF and failing EGR valve. What they thought "Standard DPF issues on a high-mileage Transit." Replace the parts, problem solved. What it actually was Failed injectors causing bore wash Worn injectors over-fuelling, washing oil from bores, destroying rings. The breaking point Oil consumption at 1 litre per 500 miles DPF warning back. £1,200 wasted. Engine replacement required. According to [KNOWN FAILURE PATTERNS] data for Ford Duratorq engines, injector failure is common between 80,000 and 150,000 miles, with symptoms including black smoke, loss of power, and failed emissions. Failure timeline £1,200 in wasted repairs - and the same problems came back within 3 months. The worn injectors were over-fuelling the engine. Unburnt diesel was washing the oil from the cylinder bores - a condition known as "bore wash." This wore the piston rings, causing excessive oil consumption. The excess fuel was also rapidly clogging the new DPF. What the manager thought "Replace the DPF and EGR. Standard high-mileage Transit issues." What it actually was Failed injectors over-fuelling for months. Killed the DPF and EGR. Wore the rings and bores. £1,200 wasted. Workshop diagnosis The specialist confirmed failed injectors, bore wash, and scored cylinders. The specialist performed a compression test, injector leak-off test, and borescope inspection. The findings were severe - the engine needed a full rebuild or replacement. Injectors (cylinders 2 & 3) Failed - excessive leak-off, poor spray pattern Piston rings Worn - bore wash damage, excessive oil consumption Cylinder bores Scoring visible on cylinder 2 DPF Rapidly clogging again - ash load high despite new unit EGR valve Carboned up Turbocharger Unknown condition - possible oil contamination from blow-by Specialist summary "The injectors failed first. They've been over-fuelling for months. That killed the DPF and EGR, and it's worn the rings and bores. You can replace the injectors and rings, but the bores are scored. This engine needs a full rebuild or replacement. The £1,200 you spent on the DPF and EGR was wasted - the injectors killed them again." Repair options Three choices: rebuild, reconditioned exchange, or new dealer engine. The specialist presented three distinct paths. For a fleet vehicle, downtime was the hidden cost that made the exchange engine the clear winner. Exchange basis. Supply cost £4,000-£6,000+ [THIRD-PARTY - Ford dealer pricing] Warranty 24 months, Ford Lead time 7-14 days Key upside Zero-mile factory engine Best for Vehicles under warranty or insurance claims The uncertainty play Bore wash creates risk beyond the visible cylinder scoring. When the specialist removed the injectors and inspected the bores, they found scoring on cylinder 2 that could be felt with a fingernail. The excessive oil consumption from the worn rings meant the turbo had been running with reduced oil quality. Path A Exchange reconditioned engine only - take the risk on the existing turbo. £3,800 If turbo fails later: add £800-£1,200 + labour. Path B Replace the turbo preventatively at the same time as the engine. £4,600 £3,800 engine + £800 turbo. Eliminates the risk entirely. The fleet manager chose Path B - prioritising reliability and uptime over upfront cost. A turbo failure on a Transit would add £800-£1,200 to the bill - plus labour and downtime.
